newsitem.title: USA: GM workers resume output at Ohio components plants.
newsitem.headline: GM workers resume output at Ohio components plants.

text.p: Striking workers at General Motors Corp.'s electrical components plants in Warren, Ohio, began to resume production on Wednesday following a tentative contract deal that provides them with improved job security.

The agreement early Wednesday ended a daylong strike by 8,200 members of the International Union of Electronics Workers, and averted a broad shutdown of GM's North American car and truck assembly operations.

The 18 Delphi Packard Electric Systems division plants in the Warren-Youngstown area produce electrical components used in vehicle wiring harnesses, instrument clusters, battery cables and other parts for nearly all of GM's North American-built vehicles.
The plants also make components for many other automakers around the world.
The IUE Local 717 members began to return to work on the first shift Wednesday in order to keep parts supplies flowing.
"By second shift we should pretty much back into a full production situation," said Delphi Packard Electric spokesman James Kobus. "There won't be any interruption" in supplies.

Union officials said they expected to have details later Wednesday on the schedule for a ratification vote. Local 717 members rejected a tentative contract agreement in March in part because it did not alter the unit's three-tier wage scale.
Local 717 President Nick Border declined to discuss the new pact in detail, but said it meets the union's goals for job security.
"Every person that is represented by this union at Delphi Packard Electric will have a guaranteed job to retire from," Border said. "Everybody wants to keep that paycheck."
The union has sought to stem GM's moving of some work to Mexico, such as the labour-intensive assembly of vehicle wiring harnesses.
Border said while the agreement does not necessarily restrict GM from moving some work to Mexico, it requires the automaker to replace that production with new work.
The strike was only the second in 26 years for the GM division, and both were short-lived. A 1971 strike lasted only 12 hours.

Kobus said it was important for Delphi Packard Electric to maintain uninterrupted production because such reliability is critical for gaining non-GM customers. The unit has the most diversified customer base of any GM parts operation, with more than half of its $5 billion in annual revenues coming outside of GM's North American automotive operations.

GM has set a goal for its entire Delphi Automotive Systems parts operation to reach the same level of diversification by 2002. Currently, about 36 percent of Delphi's sales are to customers other than GM in North America.
The Ohio settlement leaves GM with two continuing strikes at assembly plants in Oklahoma City and Pontiac, Mich.

Burnham Securities analyst David Healy estimated on Tuesday that those two walkouts so far have cost the automaker roughly 43,000 vehicles, or $194 million in lost profits. GM continues to lose about 2,300 vehicles a day to the strikes.

The Oklahoma City plant, idled since April 4, builds GM's new Chevrolet Malibu and Oldsmobile Cutlass cars, while Pontiac, which was struck on April 22, is one of three GM plants that build full-size Chevrolet and GMC pickup trucks.
